title: Next page of match history with a keyset cursor
prompt:
A game server shows each player's finished matches, newest first, four per page. OFFSET pages got slow and skipped rows when new matches finished, so the client now sends a cursor: the finished_at and id of the last match it already shows.

The cursor is stored in page_cursor (at most one row). Return the next page: the 4 matches that come after the cursor in the order finished_at newest first, then id highest first. If page_cursor is empty, return the first page.

- Columns: id, map, finished_at (formatted as text 'YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI')
- Order: finished_at descending, then id descending
- Several matches can finish at the same instant; none may be skipped or repeated across pages
- The match the cursor points to may have been deleted; still continue from its position
- Return fewer than 4 rows (or none) near the end
hints: The page order is (finished_at DESC, id DESC). 'After the cursor' means strictly smaller in that pair order.
finished_at < cursor alone skips matches that tie with the cursor's time. Compare the pair: Postgres supports row comparisons like (a, b) < (x, y).
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM page_cursor) OR (m.finished_at, m.id) < (SELECT last_finished_at, last_id FROM page_cursor) ORDER BY m.finished_at DESC, m.id DESC LIMIT 4

exercise.starter:
-- Next page after the cursor in page_cursor
SELECT id, map, to_char(finished_at, 'YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI') AS finished_at
FROM matches
ORDER BY finished_at DESC
LIMIT 4;
exercise.solution:
SELECT m.id, m.map, to_char(m.finished_at, 'YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI') AS finished_at
FROM matches m
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM page_cursor)
   OR (m.finished_at, m.id) < (SELECT c.last_finished_at, c.last_id FROM page_cursor c)
ORDER BY m.finished_at DESC, m.id DESC
LIMIT 4;

hiddenTests.name: many pages with paired ties
hiddenTests.seed:
INSERT INTO matches SELECT i, 'm' || i, timestamp '2026-10-01 00:00' + (i / 2) * interval '1 hour' FROM generate_series(1, 20) AS i;
INSERT INTO page_cursor VALUES ('2026-10-01 07:00', 14);

explanation: Keyset pagination continues from the last seen sort key instead of counting rows, so it needs a total order; id breaks ties on finished_at. The row comparison (finished_at, id) < (cursor_time, cursor_id) is true when finished_at is earlier, or equal with a smaller id, which is exactly 'after the cursor' in a descending order. The classic trap is WHERE finished_at < cursor_time, which silently skips the other matches that finished at the same instant; using <= repeats them. When page_cursor is empty the row subquery yields NULL, so the NOT EXISTS branch is what returns the first page.
notes: With the index on (finished_at DESC, id DESC), Postgres can turn the row comparison into an index range scan that starts at the cursor and stops after 4 rows, so every page costs the same. OFFSET n must read and throw away n rows, so deep pages get slower, and rows shift when new matches finish. Row comparisons only use the index well when all columns sort in the same direction; mixed directions need the expanded OR form or a different index.
followUps: How would you build a 'previous page' query from the first row currently shown?
The list must be sorted by score DESC but id ASC as the tie-breaker. How does the WHERE clause change?
